reference_title: Design and Construction of Mechanically Stabilized Earth Walls and Reinforced Soil Slopes

sections.title: Applications
sections.body: MSE walls are cost-effective alternatives for most applications where reinforced concrete or gravity walls have traditionally been used: bridge abutments, wing walls, restricted ROW embankments. They are particularly suited to steep terrain, slope instability sites, or poor foundation soils, offering savings exceeding 50% over conventional walls on poor foundation sites. Temporary MSE walls are widely used for highway reconstruction detours, temporary bridge abutments, and phased construction. Reinforced Soil Slopes (RSS) incorporate planar reinforcing elements in constructed slopes with face inclinations less than 70 degrees, providing increased slope stability and improved compaction at slope edges.
key_points: MSE walls cost-effective alternative to RC/gravity walls for abutments, wing walls, restricted ROW
Cost savings >50% over conventional walls on poor foundation sites (eliminates pile foundations)
Temporary MSE walls widely used for detours, temporary abutments, phased construction
RSS: face inclination < 70 degrees; two purposes: (1) increased slope stability, (2) improved edge compaction
RSS can reuse slide debris rather than importing higher quality fill
RSS with nonwoven geotextiles provides in-plane drainage for pore pressure dissipation in cohesive fills
sections.applicability: Selection of MSE wall or RSS for transportation retaining structures and slope stabilization.

sections.title: Advantages and Potential Disadvantages
sections.body: MSE wall advantages over conventional RC walls: simple/rapid construction with no special skills, less site preparation, less construction space, reduced ROW, tolerance to deformations without rigid foundation support, cost-effective, feasible to heights >100 ft (30 m), higher seismic resistance, and aesthetic flexibility. RSS advantages include right-of-way savings, potential use of lower quality fill (including slide debris), vegetated face for aesthetics, and inherently conservative design. Potential disadvantages for all reinforced soil structures: requires large space behind face for reinforcement installation; MSE walls require select granular fill (RSS fill requirements less restrictive); shared design responsibility between material suppliers and owners.
key_points: MSE walls more economical than other wall systems for heights >10 ft (3 m) or where special foundations required
MSE walls: flexible, tolerate differential settlement, higher seismic resistance than rigid RC walls
RSS can be constructed at about half the cost of MSEW structures
RSS designed at same FS are actually safer than unreinforced slopes (inherent conservatism)
MSE walls require select granular reinforced fill — primary disadvantage vs. flatter unreinforced slope
Reinforcement installation requires space behind wall face (may require excavation in cut situations)
sections.applicability: Project evaluation and system selection for MSE walls and RSS.

sections.title: Relative Costs
sections.body: MSE walls with precast concrete facings are usually less expensive than reinforced concrete walls for heights >10 ft (3 m) with average foundation conditions. Savings of 25 to 50% over conventional RC structures are typical, with greater savings when deep foundations are eliminated. Typical total costs for permanent transportation MSE walls range from $30 to $65/ft2 ($320 to $650/m2) of face, varying with height, size, aesthetics, accessibility, and fill cost. For segmental precast faced walls, relative component costs: erection/profit 20-30%, reinforcing materials 15-30%, facing system 20-40%, reinforced fill 30-60%. RSS bid prices range from $10 to $24/ft2 ($110 to $260/m2) as a function of height; reinforcement represents 45-65% of RSS cost.
key_points: MSE walls typically 25-50% less expensive than conventional RC retaining structures
Permanent MSE walls: $30-65/ft2 ($320-650/m2) face area — varies widely by region and fill cost
Reinforced fill (select granular) is typically 30-60% of total MSE wall cost
MBW faced walls < 15 ft (4.5 m) typically 10% or more less expensive than segmental panel walls
RSS costs $10-24/ft2 ($110-260/m2) depending on height; reinforcement is 45-65% of cost
Small projects < 3,000 ft2 (300 m2): unit cost 10-15% higher than larger projects
sections.applicability: Preliminary cost comparison between MSE walls, RSS, and conventional retaining structures.

sections.title: Description of MSE and RSS Systems
sections.body: A system is a complete supplied package including design, specifications, and all prefabricated materials. Components cannot be substituted without complete evaluation of impact on the system. MSE/RSS systems are characterized by reinforcement geometry (linear unidirectional strips/grids, composite unidirectional bar mats, planar bi-directional mesh), reinforcement material (metallic galvanized steel vs. nonmetallic polymeric), and reinforcement extensibility (inextensible: steel strips/bar mats; extensible: geogrid, geotextile, woven wire mesh). Major facing types: segmental precast concrete panels (min 5.5 in. thick, typically 5x5 or 5x10 ft), dry-cast MBW units (30-110 lbs, 4-12 in. tall, 8-24 in. deep), welded wire mesh (for RSS ≥45 degrees), gabion facing, geosynthetic facing, and post-construction facing. Steel reinforcements (ribbed strips 2 in. wide x 5/32 in. thick; welded wire grids W7.5-W24) used with precast panels. Geosynthetic reinforcements (HDPE geogrid, PVC-coated PET geogrid, geotextiles) predominantly used with MBW systems. MSE walls require high quality well-graded granular reinforced fill; RSS fill requirements are less restrictive.
key_points: Three reinforcement geometry types: linear unidirectional (strips), composite unidirectional (bar mats), planar bi-directional (mesh)
Inextensible: steel strips/bar mats; extensible: geogrids, geotextiles, woven wire (failure strain ≥ soil)
Segmental precast panels: min 5.5 in. thick, 20-50 ft2 area, AASHTO T&T reinforcement required
MBW units: 30-110 lbs, 8 in. typical height, 8-24 in. depth; dry-stacked with shear pins/lips/keys
MBW freeze-thaw durability requires specific mix design — must verify with lab testing in aggressive climates
MSE reinforced fill: well-graded granular, AASHTO T-99 compaction to 95-100%, dry of optimum
RSS fill less restrictive than MSE fill — any embankment-quality soil acceptable
sections.applicability: System selection and specification of components for MSE walls and RSS.

sections.title: Construction Sequence
sections.body: MSEW with precast panel facings: (1) subgrade preparation including removal of unsuitable material and compaction; (2) placement of unreinforced concrete leveling pad (typically 1 ft wide x 6 in. thick); (3) erection of first row of facing panels (braced); (4) compacted reinforced fill placement to first reinforcement level (loose lift max 12 in., 95-100% T-99 density); (5) placement of reinforcement layers perpendicular to face; (6) repeat for each layer; (7) construct traffic barriers and copings. Flexible-faced walls: reinforcement placed with principal strength perpendicular to face, secured with retaining pins; face wrapped with minimum 4 ft return length. RSS construction: site prep, subsurface drainage, reinforcement layer, compact backfill, face construction, additional reinforcement layers, surface drainage. Compaction within 3 ft of wall face uses hand-operated vibratory compactor to prevent panel displacement.
key_points: Leveling pad: unreinforced concrete, ~1 ft wide x 6 in. thick; not a structural foundation, only a guide
Loose lift thickness maximum 12 in. (300 mm); compact to 95-100% AASHTO T-99, dry of optimum
Reinforcements placed perpendicular to wall face; connected when fill reaches connection level
Only first tier of precast panels requires bracing; subsequent rows wedged/clamped to adjacent panels
Hand compactor required within 3 ft (~1 m) of wall face to avoid panel displacement
Flexible face: minimum 4 ft (1.25 m) return fold for pullout resistance; adjacent sheets overlap min 6 in.
sections.applicability: Construction of MSE walls and RSS for both precast panel and flexible-faced systems.

sections.title: Site Evaluation
sections.body: Site evaluation includes field reconnaissance, subsurface exploration, and laboratory testing. Borings should be located along the front and back of the structure at 100 ft (30 m) intervals along alignment and 150 ft (45 m) along the back. Boring depth should extend at least twice the wall/slope height, with rock coring to 10 ft minimum. Soil samples at 5-ft (1.5 m) intervals and at stratum changes for SPT, thin-walled tube sampling, or CPT. Groundwater levels should be monitored over time; piezometers may be needed. Laboratory tests: USCS classification, moisture-density (T-99 or T-180), shear strength (direct shear, triaxial), consolidation (if compressible foundation soils), gradation, Atterberg limits, pH (AASHTO T 289), electrical resistivity, sulfate content (AASHTO T 290), sulfide content (ASTM D4327), and chloride content (ASTM D4327).
key_points: Borings: 100 ft along wall alignment, 150 ft along back of structure; depth ≥ 2H below finished grade
Reinforced fill width ≈ 0.8H for boring layout planning
SPT (AASHTO T 206) for granular soils; thin-walled tubes (T 207) for cohesive soils
Electrochemical tests required for reinforcement durability: pH, resistivity, sulfates, sulfides, chlorides
pH < 5 or > 10 accelerates metallic reinforcement corrosion; PET degrades in highly alkaline or acidic regimes
Foundation bearing capacity, settlement potential, and groundwater position must all be evaluated
Settlement analyses critical — inadequate investigation is leading cause of MSE wall distress
sections.applicability: Subsurface investigation for MSE wall and RSS projects.

sections.title: Project Evaluation
sections.body: Structure selection factors include geologic/topographic conditions, environmental conditions, size and nature of structure, aesthetics, durability, performance criteria, material availability, experience, and cost. MSE structures are especially suited to fill-type walls and side-hill fills. For soft foundation soils, available shear strength must be ≥2.0 to 2.5 times the fill weight for vertical MSE structures. Environmental aggressiveness affects reinforcement selection: chloride/sulfate salts >200 PPM or pH <5 accelerate steel corrosion; pH >10 accelerates galvanization loss. MSE walls feasible to 135 ft (41 m) in U.S. with steel; RSS to 242 ft (74 m) with geogrids. Nominal bearing resistance of reinforced fill for service limit state typically limited to 4000 psf (200 kPa) for bridge abutments. MSE walls not suitable where utilities within reinforced zone require future cutting of reinforcements, where galvanized steel is exposed to acid mine drainage, or where floodplain erosion may undermine the reinforced fill zone.
key_points: For soft foundations: available shear strength must be ≥ 2.0-2.5 × fill weight for vertical MSE walls
Concrete-faced MSE: tolerates longitudinal differential settlement up to 1/100 without special joints
Full-height concrete panels: limit differential settlement to 1/500; MBW: 1/200; welded wire: 1/50
Minimum horizontal bench 4 ft (1.2 m) wide required in front of walls founded on slopes
Nominal bearing resistance limit: 4000 psf (200 kPa) for bridge abutment footings at service limit state
Design seismic check required for As > 0.05; deformation analysis recommended for As > 0.29g
Minimum reinforcement length: 0.7H for static loading; 0.8H for sloping backfill or seismic
sections.applicability: Project feasibility and system selection for MSE walls and RSS.

sections.title: Establishment of Project Criteria
sections.body: Project criteria development includes: considering all possible alternatives; choosing MSEW or RSS system; considering facing options; developing performance criteria (loads, design heights, embedment, settlement tolerances, foundation capacity, effect on adjoining structures); and considering corrosion/degradation effects. MSE wall design per AASHTO LRFD Article 11.10 (2007). Design life for permanent walls: minimum 75 years; 36 months for temporary walls; 100 years for walls supporting bridge abutments, buildings, or critical utilities. RSS design remains limit equilibrium based (AASHTO LRFD 2007 does not address RSS). Minimum embedment depth: H/20 for horizontal grade, H/10 for 3H:1V slope, H/7 for 2H:1V, H/5 for 1.5H:1V; absolute minimum 2 ft (0.6 m) except on rock. For scour: minimum 2 ft (0.6 m) below reliable scour depth.
key_points: Minimum design life: 75 years permanent, 36 months temporary, 100 years for bridge abutments/critical utilities
Minimum reinforcement length 0.7H; Table 2-1 gives required L/H for static, sloping backfill, and seismic
Minimum embedment depth: H/20 (horizontal), H/10 (3H:1V), H/7 (2H:1V), H/5 (1.5H:1V); min 2 ft absolute
Bench 4 ft wide required in front of walls on slopes; minimum 2 ft below scour depth for stream crossings
Traffic load per AASHTO 3.11.6.4: equivalent to 2 ft (0.6 m) of soil over traffic lanes
No upper height limit for MSE walls theoretically; practical limits from economy, ROW, and reinforcement strength
sections.applicability: Establishing design parameters and performance criteria for MSE wall and RSS projects.

sections.title: Proprietary Aspects
sections.body: Most fundamental process patents for MSE wall systems have expired. Current unexpired patents cover: connection details between grid reinforcement and precast panels (concrete-embedded connector only); most MBW facing unit designs; specific MSE construction methods under water; specific traffic barrier designs over MSE walls; and facing attachments to temporary facings. The combination of components in generic systems must be tested and evaluated together — components cannot be substituted without evaluating impact on system performance.
key_points: Fundamental process patents for MSE walls have largely expired
Current patents: grid-to-panel connections, most MBW facing units, certain special construction methods
Generic systems assembled from components must be evaluated as a complete system
Component substitution requires full re-evaluation of system compatibility and performance
sections.applicability: Procurement and approval of MSE wall systems for transportation projects.

sections.title: Case Histories — MSE Walls
sections.body: Mn/DOT Crosstown Project (Minneapolis, MN): ~300,000 ft2 of MSE walls in 24 separate walls, heights 25-45 ft, steel bar mat reinforcement with architectural precast panels, 100-year design life, cost $54.50/ft2 including fill and moment slab vs. $76/ft2 for CIP walls. Veterans Memorial Overpass (Tucson, AZ): 25- and 35-ft high true bridge abutments, 150 ft long, ribbed steel strips with 5x10 ft precast panels; dense underlying soils, <1 in. settlement during construction. SeaTac Airport Runway Extension: tallest MSE wall in U.S. at time of construction, 138 ft (42 m) exposed height, 150 ft (46 m) constructed height, 1430 ft (436 m) long, steel strips with precast panels. Guanella Pass (Colorado Rockies): 21 wire-faced walls totaling ~12,000 ft length on steep slopes (1.3H:1V to 1.5H:1V), reinforcement lengths 70-120% of wall height, successfully used on-site soils with up to 20% passing No. 200 sieve.
key_points: Mn/DOT Crosstown: MSE $54.50/ft2 vs. CIP walls $76/ft2 — 28% cost savings with comparable performance
SeaTac: tallest U.S. MSE wall — 138 ft exposed, 150 ft constructed; steel strips with precast panels
Guanella Pass: MSE walls on 1.3-1.5H:1V slopes; reinforcement lengths up to 1.2H; 20% fines allowed
All case histories show MSE wall tolerance to difficult conditions (settlement, steep slopes, remote sites)
Geomembrane across top of reinforced zone can prevent de-icing salt infiltration (Mn/DOT example)
sections.applicability: Reference case histories for MSE wall performance and cost on transportation projects.
